Learning Objectives
Assess primary medial approaches to the knee joint, including the medial parapatellar,
midvastus, and subvastus approaches.
Determine the indications for more advanced exposure techniques during primary and
revision total knee arthroplasty.
Describe the rehabilitation changes after a quadriceps snip and a tibial tubercle osteotomy.

The Wiberg classification includes three types.
Type 1: medial and lateral facets are equal in size
Type 2: most common type; medial facet is smaller and one-half the size of the lateral facet.
Type 3: medial facet is so far medial that the central ridge barely is noticeable.

Osteology
The posterior slope of the tibia is a mean of 10.7° in the medial plateau and 7.2° in the
lateral plateau; however, these slopes vary widely in nonarthritic knees.1,2 The medial
compartment has a large surface area and contains the convex larger medial femoral
condyle and the concave tibial plateau. The lateral compartment has a smaller surface
area than the medial compartment and contains the convex and smaller lateral femoral
condyle and the convex lateral plateau (sagittal plane). The tibial tuberosity is located
slightly lateral to the midline of the knee and is the site of attachment of the patellar
tendon. The Gerdy tubercle is located 2 to 3 cm lateral to the tibial tuberosity and is the
site of insertion of the iliotibial band. The fibular head is located a mean of 1.5 cm distal
to the joint line; however, this distance varies widely (range, 6 to 32 mm).
The femur is composed of two condyles. The medial femoral condyle has a large, convex
articular surface. The medial collateral ligament (MCL) originates from the femoral sulcus
of the medial femoral condyle, approximately 3.2 cm proximal and 4.8 cm posterior to
the articular surface of the femur at the knee. The adductor tubercle is a prominence on
the medial condyle proximal to the MCL origin and is the site of insertion of the adductor
magnus muscle.3,4
The lateral femoral condyle size varies and has a convex articular surface. This condyle is
wider than the medial femoral condyle in the anterior-posterior and medial-lateral
dimensions, which allows for internal/external rotation. The sulcus terminalis is a
transverse ridge extending from the oblique facets of the femoral trochlea and is the
distalmost extent of the patellar articulation with the femur. The sulcus terminalis is
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:42 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001029
3/32

deeper on the lateral condyle than on the medial condyle. Patellar tracking occurs
through the femoral trochlea located on the anterior surface of the femur.
The patella is a large sesamoid bone with a mean thickness of 2.5 cm. The three patellar
facets include the lateral, medial, and odd facets. The odd facet is a small facet on the
distal medial patella that articulates in deep flexion of the knee. Patellar morphology has
been previously described.5
Vascular Anatomy
The blood supply to the knee is formed from the anastomosis of several branches of the
genicular artery (Figure 2).
The descending geniculate artery arises from the femoral artery.
The medial and lateral superior geniculate arteries arise from the popliteal artery.
The medial and lateral inferior geniculate arteries arise from the popliteal artery.
Pass deep to their respective collateral ligaments
At risk for persistent bleeding after meniscectomy
The middle geniculate artery arises from the popliteal artery and provides the blood supply
to the cruciate ligaments.
Anterior tibial recurrent arteries

Vascular Anatomy
The primary blood supply to the knee is from the popliteal artery, a branch of the
femoral artery. Surrounding the knee, a rich anastomosis of vessels is primarily supplied
by branches of the femoral and popliteal arteries. The femoral artery supplies the
descending genicular artery and then enters the adductor canal. On exiting the adductor
canal, the femoral artery transitions into the popliteal artery and traverses the posterior
aspect of the knee. The popliteal artery branches into the medial and lateral superior

tibia.6
Nerves
Femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4)
Infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve
Disrupted during standard approaches to the knee
Obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4)
Sciatic nerve (L4, L5, S1, S2)
Peroneal nerve
Potential nerve injury is related to lateral releases performed in patients with a valgus knee
deformity.

Nerves
The largest nerve of the knee is the posterior articular branch of the posterior tibial
nerve, which innervates the infrapatellar fat pad, synovial covering of the cruciate
ligaments, and periphery of the meniscus. The peroneal nerve courses deep to the
biceps femoris tendon, distal to the fibular collateral ligament as it crosses the joint line
of the knee, and courses around the fibular head to enter the anterior compartment of
the knee (Figure 3). The peroneal nerve is at highest risk of injury during lateral releases
performed for valgus total knee arthroplasty.7 The infrapatellar branch of the saphenous
nerve arises proximal to the knee joint medially and crosses distal to the patella to
innervate the skin over the anterior knee and tibia. This nerve branch can become
entrapped between the sartorius tendon and the medial femoral condyle.

Blood supply: middle geniculate artery
Prevents anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur.
Two bundles

Posterolateral bundle is tight in knee extension and lax in flexion.
Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL)
Blood supply: middle geniculate artery
Prevents posterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur
Anterolateral bundle is tight in knee flexion and lax in extension.

Posteromedial bundle is tight in knee extension and lax in flexion.
Menisci
Primary blood supply: geniculate arteries
Attached to the collateral ligaments via the coronary ligaments
The lateral meniscus is circular, and medial meniscus is crescent shaped.
Popliteal tendon
Laterally based tendon that courses through the popliteal hiatus
Occasionally released during total knee arthroplasty in patients with severe valgus
deformities.
Meniscofemoral ligaments
Two ligaments
Insertion site is the PCL and originate from the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus
Ligament of Humphry (anterior)
Ligament of Wrisberg (posterior)

Intra-Articular Anatomy
The ACL consists of 90% type I collagen and 10% type III collagen. It has a mean length of
33 mm and a mean width of 11 mm. The femoral attachment is on the posteromedial
aspect of the lateral femoral condyle (mean length, 20 mm; mean width, 10 mm). A
broad, irregular, oval-shaped insertion is present on the tibia between the tibial
eminences from anterior to midline. The middle geniculate artery is the primary blood
supply. The posterior articular branch of the posterior tibial nerve provides innervation.
The anteromedial bundle is tight in knee flexion, and the posterolateral bundle is tight in
knee extension.8 The posterolateral bundle of the ACL is responsible for preventing the
pivot-shift phenomenon and stabilizes against anterior translation with 30° of knee
flexion.
The anteromedial bundle of the ACL resists anterior tibial translation at 60° and 90° of
knee flexion. To approximate normal kinematics of the knee joint, some surgeons
advocate for restoration of both ACL bundles. The most commonly reported reason for
ACL graft failure is malpositioning of bone tunnels during an approach in which a single
femoral tunnel is used.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:42 AM
AAOS | Surgical Anatomy of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001029
8/32

The PCL has a mean length of 38 mm and a mean width of 13 mm. A broad, crescent-
shaped femoral attachment is present on the anterolateral medial femoral condyle. The
tibial insertion onto the posterior central sulcus is 10 to 15 mm distal to the knee joint
line. The middle geniculate artery is the primary blood supply. The popliteal artery is in
close proximity to the PCL, and the distance increases with knee flexion. The posterior
articular branch of the posterior tibial nerve provides innervation. The anterolateral
bundle (stronger/stiffer than the posteromedial bundle) is tight in knee flexion, and the
posteromedial bundle is tight in knee extension.9
The menisci are crescent-shaped, fibrocartilaginous structures with a triangular cross
section. They consist of type I collagen fibers arranged obliquely, radially, and vertically.
The vascular supply is derived from the geniculate arteries, which penetrate into 20% to
30% of the peripheral medial meniscus and 10% to 25% of the peripheral lateral
meniscus. The menisci are attached to collateral ligaments via the coronary ligaments.
The medial meniscus is crescent shaped and attaches more anterior and posterior.10
The lateral meniscus is circular and covers a larger proportion of the tibial plateau, and
its anterior attachment is adjacent to the tibial insertion of the ACL.
The popliteal tendon originates on the posterocentral tibia. It inserts anterior and distal
to the lateral collateral ligament (LCL) on the lateral femoral epicondyle. The popliteal
tendon has an intra-articular course through the popliteal hiatus.
Two meniscofemoral ligaments exist: the ligament of Humphry (anterior) and the
ligament of Wrisberg (posterior). At least a single ligament is present in 93% of the
population, and two ligaments are present in 70% of the population. The
meniscofemoral ligaments insert into the substance of the PCL and the medial femoral
condyle and originate from the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus.11
Extra-Articular Anatomy
Medial knee
The medial knee has three primary layers.

The third layer is composed of the joint capsule, deep MCL, and coronary ligaments.

The MCL has two parts: the superficial and deep MCL. The superficial MCL (tibial
collateral ligament) is deep to the semitendinosus and gracilis tendons. The origin of the
superficial MCL is on the medial femoral condyle (sulcus) and inserts broadly 4 to 6 cm
distal to the joint line on the tibia. The mean length is 9.5 cm. The anterior fibers tighten
during the first 90° of knee flexion, and the posterior fibers tension with knee
extension.12
The deep MCL (medial capsular ligament) blends with the superficial fibers distally. The
deep MCL is associated with the medial meniscus through the coronary ligament. The
primary blood supply is from the superomedial and inferomedial geniculate arteries. The
greatest laxity of the deep MCL is at 30° of knee flexion. In extension, stability relies on
the posterior capsule.
The medial patellofemoral ligament originates 1.9 mm anterior and 3.8 mm distal to the
adductor tubercle. It inserts onto the superomedial patella and stabilizes against lateral
patellar displacement.
The oblique popliteal ligament consists of a thickening of the posterior and
posteromedial capsule. It is the largest posterior ligamentous structure and extends
from the superolateral capsule behind the lateral femoral condyle to the
semimembranosus tendon insertion.
The posterior oblique ligament originates 7.7 mm distal and 6.4 mm posterior to the
adductor tubercle. This ligament stabilizes the medial meniscus and provides
posteromedial rotatory stability to the knee.
The superficial layer contains the biceps femoris muscle and the iliotibial band. The
biceps femoris originates from the ischium and the posterior femur and inserts onto the
fibular head posterior to the ligamentous complexes. The biceps femoris lies anterior to
the common peroneal nerve. The iliotibial band originates from the lateral ilium (tensor
fascia latae and gluteus maximus muscles) and inserts onto the Gerdy tubercle.
The LCL originates posterior and superior to the popliteal tendon and is located 1.4 mm
proximal and 3.4 mm posterior to the lateral femoral epicondylar ridge. The LCL inserts

on the lateral fibular head (3 to 4 mm in diameter), and its mean length is 66 mm. The
blood supply is from the inferolateral and superolateral geniculate arteries. The LCL
inserts at the most anterior point of the fibular head, and the biceps femoris tendon
inserts on the most posterior point.
The capsule extends from the popliteal tendon insertion to the lateral gastrocnemius-
soleus complex attachment. The middle one-third of the capsular ligament divides into
the meniscofemoral and meniscotibial ligaments. A Segond fracture involves avulsion of
the meniscotibial ligament and may contribute to a fixed valgus deformity.
The popliteofibular ligament connects the popliteal muscle to the posteromedial fibula
and has anterior and posterior divisions. This ligament stabilizes the knee against
external rotation.
The fabellofibular ligament originates from the fabella (variable presence) and inserts
onto the fibular head.
The arcuate ligament originates from the styloid process of the fibula and inserts on the
femur, contiguous with the oblique popliteal ligament.
In extension, the iliotibial band and the LCL are commonly associated with valgus
contracture. In flexion, the joint capsule, popliteal tendon, posterolateral ligaments, and
LCL are associated with valgus deformity.

medial and lateral retinacular extensions, and patellar tendon. The quadriceps muscle
has four components.

The patellar tendon has a mean width of 3.2 cm at its origin on the patella and 2.7 cm at
its insertion on the tibial tuberosity. Its length varies from 38 to 49 mm, and it has an
extended insertion on the tibial tuberosity.
Blood Supply
Skin
 Anastomosis of vessels in the deep fascia
The vessels supply the subcutaneous fat and epidermis from deep to superficial.13 These
vessels are found predominantly medially; therefore, dissection should remain deep to this
layer to prevent disruption of the blood supply to the superficial layers (Figure 8).

by the deep vessels (solid circles indicate the approximate position of deep perforators). Most of
the blood supply comes from the medial side; therefore, the use of a medial incision will increase

Blood Supply
During a medial parapatellar approach, the three medial vascular sources are
disrupted.14 In addition, the inferior lateral genicular artery may be divided during
removal of the lateral meniscus. Often, the anterior recurrent tibial artery is disrupted
during removal of the patellar fat pad. Therefore, the superior lateral genicular may be
the only viable blood supply to the patella during a standard medial parapatellar
approach to the knee. Caution should be used in performing an internal lateral release
(to improve patellar tracking) to avoid damaging the superior lateral genicular artery.
Inadvertent disruption may lead to patellar osteonecrosis.
Physical Examination
Inspection
Location of prior incisions
Angle of prior incisions
Range of motion

Physical Examination
The physical examination is a key component in determining the location and type of
surgical exposure required for each patient. Particular attention should focus on the
location of previous scars around the knee. Commonly, the most lateral knee incision

allowing access to the knee joint should be used. This decision is secondary to
considering the blood supply originating medially. Incisions that traverse the knee joint
horizontally may compromise the skin’s healing potential. These incisions should be
incorporated if possible or crossed perpendicular to minimize skin breakdown. Finally,
extremely limited range of motion may require more advanced exposure techniques,
such as a rectus snip or a tibial tubercle osteotomy.
Primary Surgical Approaches
Skin Incision
Use the most lateral skin incision that allows access to the joint.
Bridge prior skin incisions by approximately 7 cm if the prior incision cannot be used.
Make the incision medial to the tibial tubercle.
Make the incision 5 to 10 cm proximal to the superior pole of the patella.
Minimize skin flaps but, if necessary, develop full-thickness skin flaps.

Skin Incision
If prior incisions are present, use the most lateral skin incision that can still provide
access to the joint. In addition, if prior skin incisions cross the standard skin incision,
incorporate them into the incision. The incision begins just medial to the medial edge of
the tibial tubercle and is extended proximally 5 to 10 cm proximal to the superior pole of
the patella. The incision should be carried sharply down to the extensor mechanism
before undermining the soft tissue medially or laterally. Full-thickness flaps will prevent
disruption of the superficial blood supply.
Medial Parapatellar Approach
Predominant approach for primary and revision total knee arthroplasty.
Make the incision medial to the tibial tubercle, progressing proximally along the medial
patellar tendon to the patella (Figure 9).

The incision continues proximally into the quadriceps tendon, leaving a 3- to 5-mm cuff of
quadriceps tendon on the vastus medialis.
The patella is dislocated laterally to expose the knee.

Medial Parapatellar Approach
The medial parapatellar approach is the standard approach for primary and revision
total knee arthroplasty. The incision begins just medial to the tibial tubercle and is made
along the medial border of the patellar tendon, tracking proximally to the medial border
of the patella. A 3- to 5-mm cuff of retinacular tissue should remain on the medial border
of the patella for closure. The incision is then carried proximally an additional 5 to 10 cm
into the medial border of the quadriceps tendon, with a 3- to 5-mm cuff of quadriceps
tendon medially. The patella should be able to dislocate laterally, allowing access to the
knee joint. If access is still not possible, more advanced surgical approaches can be used.
The medial capsule is then subperiosteally pealed from the patella from lateral to
medial. The remainder of the proximal and distal incisions is the same and should allow
for exposure of the joint.
The midvastus approach is similar to the medial parapatellar approach (Figure 10). The
distal two-thirds of the midvastus approach is the same as that for the medial
parapatellar approach; however, proximally, the incision exits midway up the vastus
medialis tendon into and in line with the fibers of the vastus medialis muscle. Blunt
dissection should be performed more than 1.5 cm from the quadriceps femoris tendon.

The subvastus approach also is very similar to the midvastus and medial parapatellar
approaches.16 The distal one-third of the subvastus approach is the same as that for the
medial parapatellar approach; however, proximally, the incision exits along the inferior
border of the vastus medialis tendon. The intermuscular septum is divided proximally
until the patella can be dislocated laterally. Conversion to an extensile approach may be
a challenge. If the approach may need to be extended, a tibial tubercle osteotomy may
be necessary. The subvastus approach spares the entire quadriceps muscle and may
offer faster rehabilitation. Exposure may be more difficult in large patients and in

Lateral Parapatellar Approach
Rarely used; occasionally used for the management of valgus knees and for lateral partial knee
arthroplasty.
The skin incision is based along the lateral aspect of the tibial tubercle and carried proximally 5
to 10 cm above the proximal pole of the patella.
The arthrotomy begins lateral to the tibial tubercle and is carried proximally along the lateral
patellar tendon.
The arthrotomy continues proximally lateral to the patella, and a 3- to 5-mm cuff of tissue
remains on the patella.
The arthrotomy ends proximally as the incision is extended into the lateral one-third of the
quadriceps tendon.

Lateral Parapatellar Approach
The lateral parapatellar approach is infrequently used; However, some surgeons prefer
this approach for the treatment of patients with severe valgus deformity or for lateral
unicompartmental partial knee arthroplasty. The skin incision begins just lateral to the
lateral edge of the tibial tubercle and is extended proximally 5 to 10 cm proximal to the
superior pole of the patella. The arthrotomy begins just lateral to the tibial tubercle, is
made along the lateral border of the patellar tendon, and continues proximally to the
lateral border of the patella. A 3- to 5-mm cuff of retinacular tissue should remain on the
lateral border of the patella for closure. The incision is then carried proximally an
additional 5 to 10 cm into the lateral border of the quadriceps tendon, with a 3- to 5-mm
cuff of quadriceps tendon laterally.

Extensile Exposures
The quadriceps snip is one of the most frequently used extensile exposures and allows
for excellent exposure during most revision procedures.17 The procedure involves a
superolateral (oblique) extension of the incision from the medial parapatellar
arthrotomy from the superior aspect of the quadriceps tendon into the lateral aspect of
the rectus femoris tendon. Proximally, the split is carried in line with the fibers of the
vastus lateralis. One of the biggest advantages of the quadriceps snip over other
extensile approaches is that the exposure can be primarily repaired and does not
require any change in postoperative rehabilitation.
A tibial tubercle osteotomy is another extensile exposure technique that can be
performed in combination with a medial parapatellar arthrotomy to improve exposure.
The procedures involves an 8- to 10-cm osteotomy performed from the medial tibia
beginning just below the joint line and is commonly performed with the use of an
oscillating saw through the proximal medial tibia and directed laterally.18 The saw
should not disrupt the lateral soft-tissue attachments/blood supply. The osteotomy can
subsequently be hinged laterally. The tibial tubercle osteotomy can be used to expose
metaphyseal cones and sleeves and to remove well-fixed cemented/cementless stems.
Other common indications for tibial tubercle osteotomy include patients with patella
baja or who have undergone prior patellar realignment procedures. Fixation usually is
accomplished with the use of cerclage wires or screws. Immobilization in extension for 4
to 6 weeks is recommended to allow for union of the osteotomy before beginning
physical therapy.
The quadriceps turndown involves a standard medial parapatellar arthrotomy. At the
proximal extent of the quadriceps tendon, an inverted V extension is made in the lateral
one-third of the quadriceps tendon. Exposure ends proximal to the superolateral
genicular artery to attempt to minimize the risk of patellar osteonecrosis. The major risks
associated with this approach are postoperative extensor lag and patellar osteonecrosis.
Immobilization in extension is recommended for 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively.

A medial femoral epicondyle osteotomy may aid in the management of severe, fixed
varus deformities. The procedure involves epicondyle removal along with the attached
MCL and soft tissues to preserve its blood supply. The epicondyle is subsequently
reattached. This is an infrequently used extensile exposure technique and may be
associated with nonunion or malunion of the medial epicondyle. Subsequent MCL
instability is a substantial postoperative concern.
The lateral femoral epicondyle osteotomy is not commonly used; however, it is included
for historical context and was previously occasionally used in patients with severe valgus
deformity.19 Risks included devascularization of the lateral epicondyle, instability,
nonunion, and malunion. Commonly, other exposure techniques are associated with
substantially less risk.
